triage.name: Chest Pain
triage.reason: Classic undifferentiated symptom with a broad, high-stakes differential (ACS, PE, dissection, GERD, musculoskeletal) reachable by history, exam, ECG and labs.

demographics: Chest pain is one of the most common reasons for emergency department visits in the US

The mix of causes shifts with age: younger patients more often have musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, or anxiety-related causes, while older patients more often have coronary or other cardiopulmonary causes
Men tend to present with chest pain from coronary causes at younger ages than women

risk_factors.text: Coronary artery disease or prior myocardial infarction
Family history of premature coronary artery disease
Recent immobilization, surgery, or long travel (venous thromboembolism risk)
Recent heavy lifting or new strenuous exercise

family_history: Premature coronary artery disease in a first-degree relative
Sudden cardiac death in a first-degree relative
Venous thromboembolism in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: I have pain in my chest
It feels like pressure or tightness in the middle of my chest
The pain gets worse when I breathe in or lie down
I feel like I can't catch my breath

hpi.onset: Varies by cause: sudden and maximal at onset suggests a vascular or pulmonary event, while gradual onset over minutes to hours is more typical of coronary or gastrointestinal causes
hpi.duration: From minutes to weeks depending on cause; cardiac pain often lasts minutes to tens of minutes, while musculoskeletal and gastrointestinal pain can persist for days
hpi.progression: May be constant, intermittent, or crescendo; pain that is worsening or occurring at rest is concerning for an acute coronary syndrome
hpi.location: Often substernal or left-sided, but can be anywhere in the chest, epigastrium, back, or shoulders
hpi.radiation: May radiate to the left arm, both arms, jaw, neck, back, or epigastrium
hpi.quality: Described as pressure, tightness, squeezing, heaviness, burning, sharp, or tearing depending on the cause
hpi.severity: Ranges from mild discomfort to severe; severity alone does not distinguish dangerous from benign causes
hpi.timing: May be exertional, postprandial, positional, pleuritic, or constant

associated_symptoms.text: Heartburn or sour taste in the mouth
Pain worsened by movement or breathing

pertinent_negatives: Tearing pain radiating to the back
Pain that is maximal at the very first instant
Unilateral leg swelling or calf pain
Pain reproduced only by pressing on the chest wall
Symptoms that resolve completely with antacids

argues_against: Pain that is purely positional and reproducible on chest wall palpation
Pleuritic pain with clear lungs and no dyspnea

positives.text: Pain after meals or when lying down

argues_against: Pain clearly related to meals and relieved by antacids

positives.text: Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest

argues_against: Pain that is constant and not reproducible with movement or palpation

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress, speaking in full sentences
general.moderate: Mild distress, diaphoretic, prefers to sit upright
general.severe: Marked distress, pale and diaphoretic, speaking in short sentences
general.critical: Toxic or moribund, altered mental status, unable to speak, may be hypotensive or unresponsive

findings.maneuver: Palpate the anterior chest wall, including the sternum, costochondral junctions, and pectoral muscles
findings.finding: Reproducible tenderness that recreates the patient's pain

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields and percuss the chest
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds without crackles, wheezes, or dullness

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart, palpate the precordium, and assess jugular venous pressure
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, normal JVP

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen and auscultate bowel sounds
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly or masses

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the lower extremities for edema, calf tenderness, and asymmetry
findings.finding: No unilateral swelling, calf tenderness, or edema

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin for pallor, diaphoresis, rash, or ecchymoses
findings.finding: Warm, dry, normal color, no rash

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation, attention, and level of consciousness
findings.finding: Alert and oriented, normal attention

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam including cranial nerves, strength, and sensation
findings.finding: No focal deficits

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx and neck for swelling or lymphadenopathy
findings.finding: No swelling, erythema, or lymphadenopathy

findings.maneuver: Palpate the neck for tracheal deviation, subcutaneous emphysema, and lymphadenopathy
findings.finding: Trachea midline, no crepitus or masses

findings.maneuver: Palpate cervical, supraclavicular, and axillary lymph nodes
findings.finding: No lymphadenopathy

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the genitalia if indicated by history
findings.finding: No abnormalities

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam if gastrointestinal bleeding is suspected
findings.finding: No masses, normal tone, no blood

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the breasts if breast pathology is suspected
findings.finding: No masses, skin changes, or nipple discharge

findings.maneuver: Perform a pelvic exam if a gynecologic cause is suspected
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness, adnexal masses, or discharge

labs.caveat: Normal or mildly elevated in non-cardiac chest pain; a rise or fall on serial sampling defines acute myocardial injury. Values are assay-dependent.
Normal in most non-PE chest pain; a negative result in a low-risk patient helps exclude pulmonary embolism. Nonspecific and rises with age, inflammation, pregnancy, and recent surgery.
Elevated when chest pain is from decompensated heart failure; normal in most other causes.
Leukocytosis suggests pneumonia, pericarditis, or another inflammatory cause rather than ischemia.
Supports an inflammatory cause such as pericarditis; not useful for ruling in or out acute coronary syndrome.
Elevated with shock, severe sepsis, or mesenteric ischemia; normal in most chest pain.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or medications that are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Ordered only when the pain is epigastric or radiates to the back and pancreatitis is a consideration.
Elevated with rhabdomyolysis or severe muscle injury; not a cardiac marker when troponin is available.

findings.finding: Sinus rhythm
Tachycardia
ST-segment elevation in a coronary distribution with reciprocal depression
ST-segment depression or dynamic T-wave inversion
Hyperacute peaked T waves early in infarction
Diffuse PR-segment depression and diffuse concave ST elevation
Electrical alternans with low-voltage QRS
New left bundle branch block
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Nonspecific ST-T changes

findings.text: Clear lungs with normal heart size and no mediastinal widening

imaging.study: CT angiography of the chest with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection

findings.text: Filling defect in a pulmonary artery
Intimal flap dividing the aortic lumen
No pulmonary embolism or aortic abnormality

imaging.preferred_when: High-risk acute coronary syndrome or positive stress testing

findings.text: Critical stenosis or occlusion of a coronary artery

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pulmonary embolism with contraindication to standard CTA

findings.text: Filling defect in the pulmonary arterial tree

initial.why: First test in any chest pain; identifies ST elevation, ischemia, or arrhythmia
Detects myocardial injury; serial sampling distinguishes acute from chronic elevation
Looks for anemia or leukocytosis suggesting infection
Assesses electrolytes, renal function, and glucose
Screens for pneumonia, pneumothorax, effusion, and mediastinal widening
Rules out pregnancy before imaging and medications

confirmatory.test: CT angiography of the chest with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Confirms pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection
confirmatory.only_if: pulmonary embolism or dissection is suspected

confirmatory.why: Defines coronary anatomy and allows intervention
confirmatory.only_if: high-risk acute coronary syndrome or positive stress testing

supporting.why: Negative result helps exclude pulmonary embolism in low-risk patients
supporting.only_if: pulmonary embolism is suspected and pretest probability is low

supporting.why: Supports heart failure as the cause
Supports an inflammatory cause such as pericarditis

supporting.only_if: pain is epigastric or radiates to the back

supporting.why: Assesses wall motion, valves, and pericardial effusion
supporting.only_if: murmur, heart failure, or pericardial effusion is suspected

not_indicated.why: Troponin is the preferred cardiac marker

decision_points: Obtain an ECG within 10 minutes of arrival for suspected acute coronary syndrome
Serial troponin testing rather than a single value to detect acute myocardial injury
Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Do not delay reperfusion for a patient with ST elevation on ECG

differential.name: Acute coronary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Substernal pressure with exertion, radiation to the arm or jaw, and diaphoresis is the classic presentation and the most dangerous common cause
differential.trigger: Pressure-like pain with exertion, radiation, diaphoresis, or any patient with coronary risk factors

history: Radiation to left arm, jaw, or back
exam: Signs of heart failure such as crackles or elevated jugular venous pressure
ecg: ST-segment depression or dynamic T-wave inversion
imaging: Regional wall motion abnormality on echocardiography

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea and tachycardia in a patient with venous thromboembolism risk factors
differential.trigger: Pleuritic pain with dyspnea, tachycardia, or hypoxemia in a patient with immobilization, surgery, travel, or prior venous thromboembolism

history: Recent surgery, immobilization, or long travel
Prior venous thromboembolism or active cancer
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to the pain
labs: Elevated troponin or BNP with right ventricular strain
ecg: Right axis deviation or right bundle branch block
imaging: Filling defect in a pulmonary artery on CT angiography

differential.name: Aortic dissection
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe chest or back pain, often in a patient with hypertension or connective tissue disease
differential.trigger: Abrupt, maximal-at-onset tearing pain radiating to the back, or a pulse or blood pressure differential between arms

history: Sudden onset, maximal at the first instant
Radiation to the back or between the shoulder blades
Known hypertension or connective tissue disorder
exam: Blood pressure or pulse differential between arms
Hypotension with a normal or high heart rate
labs: No single lab excludes dissection; troponin may be mildly elevated if the coronary ostium is involved
ecg: ST elevation if the dissection involves a coronary ostium

differential.name: Pericarditis
differential.why_considered: Sharp, positional chest pain that improves when sitting forward, often after a viral illness

history: Worse when lying flat, better when sitting forward
exam: Muffled heart sounds if effusion is large
labs: Elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
ecg: Electrical alternans with low-voltage QRS if tamponade

differential.name: Pneumothorax
differential.why_considered: Sudden one-sided pleuritic pain with dyspnea, especially in a tall thin young person or after trauma
differential.trigger: Sudden unilateral pleuritic pain with dyspnea and decreased breath sounds on one side

exam: Decreased breath sounds on the affected side
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side if tension
Hypotension and distended neck veins if tension
imaging: Visible pleural line with no lung markings beyond it on chest x-ray
Large pneumothorax with mediastinal shift on CT

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Pleuritic chest pain with fever, cough, and sputum production

exam: Crackles or egophony over a focal area

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Burning substernal pain after meals or when lying down, common in younger patients without coronary risk factors

differential.name: Costochondritis
differential.why_considered: Sharp chest pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall, common in younger patients

history: Pain with movement, twisting, or reaching
exam: Reproducible tenderness at the costochondral junctions or sternum

differential.name: Panic attack
differential.why_considered: Chest tightness with palpitations, dyspnea, and a sense of doom, often in younger patients with anxiety

history: Rapid onset with peak within minutes
Palpitations, trembling, and fear of dying

severity.mild: Intermittent discomfort, no distress, normal vital signs, able to speak in full sentences, no red-flag features
severity.moderate: Persistent pain with mild distress, tachycardia or mild hypoxemia, but hemodynamically stable
severity.severe: Marked distress, diaphoresis, hypoxemia, hypotension, or ECG changes suggesting acute coronary syndrome or another high-risk cause
severity.critical: Hemodynamic instability, altered mental status, respiratory failure, or cardiac arrest from a life-threatening cause such as dissection, massive pulmonary embolism, or tension pneumothorax

red_flags.finding: Pressure-like pain with diaphoresis, nausea, or radiation to the arm or jaw
red_flags.meaning: Acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise; obtain ECG within 10 minutes

red_flags.finding: Sudden tearing pain maximal at onset radiating to the back, or a blood pressure differential between arms
red_flags.meaning: Aortic dissection; needs immediate imaging and surgical consultation

red_flags.finding: Pleuritic pain with dyspnea, tachycardia, and hypoxemia in a patient with venous thromboembolism risk factors
Hypotension with distended neck veins and unilateral absent breath sounds
red_flags.meaning: Tension pneumothorax; needs immediate needle decompression
Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction; do not delay reperfusion

red_flags.finding: New murmur of aortic regurgitation or a focal neurologic deficit
Syncope or near-syncope with chest pain
red_flags.meaning: High-risk cause such as arrhythmia, massive pulmonary embolism, or dissection

complications.name: Anxiety and functional limitation after a benign cause

special_populations.differences: May present without classic chest pain, instead with dyspnea, weakness, syncope, or confusion; coronary causes are more likely and atypical presentations are common.
Autonomic neuropathy can blunt or eliminate anginal pain, so myocardial ischemia may present silently or with dyspnea alone.

Pregnancy increases venous thromboembolism risk, so pulmonary embolism and peripartum cardiomyopathy should be considered; imaging decisions must account for fetal safety, and a pregnancy test is required before CT.
Chest pain in children is usually musculoskeletal, respiratory, or anxiety-related; cardiac causes are rare but include myocarditis, pericarditis, and congenital coronary anomalies.
Infection risk is higher and presentations may be blunted; pneumonia and other opportunistic infections should be considered earlier.
Higher risk of coronary disease and pericarditis; contrast imaging requires careful consideration of kidney function.

key_questions.question: When did the pain start, and was it sudden or gradual?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden and maximal at the first instant suggests aortic dissection or pulmonary embolism; gradual onset over minutes is more typical of coronary or gastrointestinal causes

key_questions.question: What does the pain feel like — pressure, tightness, squeezing, burning, sharp, or tearing?
key_questions.looking_for: Pressure or squeezing suggests ischemia; tearing suggests dissection; burning suggests reflux; sharp and pleuritic suggests pericarditis, pneumothorax, or pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and does it go anywhere else?
key_questions.looking_for: Substernal pain radiating to the left arm, jaw, or back suggests acute coronary syndrome; radiation to the back between the shoulder blades suggests dissection

key_questions.question: What brings it on and what makes it better?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertional onset relieved by rest or nitroglycerin suggests ischemia; relief with antacids suggests reflux; improvement leaning forward suggests pericarditis

key_questions.question: Is the pain worse when you breathe in, cough, or lie flat?
key_questions.looking_for: Pleuritic pain suggests pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia, or pericarditis; worse lying flat and better sitting forward suggests pericarditis

key_questions.question: Does pressing on your chest wall reproduce the pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Reproducible chest wall tenderness suggests costochondritis or musculoskeletal pain, though it does not fully exclude a cardiac cause

key_questions.question: How long does each episode last?
key_questions.looking_for: Minutes to tens of minutes suggests angina; seconds suggests a non-cardiac cause; hours to days suggests musculoskeletal or gastrointestinal pain

key_questions.question: Are you short of breath, sweaty, nauseated, or lightheaded with the pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Diaphoresis, nausea, and dyspnea raise concern for acute coronary syndrome; dyspnea with pleuritic pain raises concern for pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Have you coughed up any blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Hemoptysis suggests pulmonary embolism or pneumonia

key_questions.question: Have you fainted or felt like you might pass out?
key_questions.looking_for: Syncope or near-syncope suggests a high-risk cause such as arrhythmia, massive pulmonary embolism, or dissection

key_questions.question: Do you have any leg swelling or calf pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral leg swelling or calf tenderness suggests deep vein thrombosis with pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent surgery, hospitalization, long travel, or immobilization?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent surgery, hospitalization, long travel, or immobilization raises venous thromboembolism risk and points toward pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of heart disease, heart attack, diabetes, high blood pressure, or high cholesterol?
key_questions.looking_for: Coronary risk factors raise the pretest probability of acute coronary syndrome

key_questions.question: Have you had a blood clot in your leg or lung before, or do you have cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior venous thromboembolism or active cancer raises pulmonary embolism risk

key_questions.question: Do you have reflux or heartburn, and does food or lying down bring on the pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Known reflux with postprandial or positional burning pain suggests a gastrointestinal cause

key_questions.question: Do you take birth control pills, hormone replacement, or any stimulants such as cocaine or amphetamines?
key_questions.looking_for: Estrogen-containing contraceptives and hormone therapy raise venous thromboembolism risk; cocaine and amphetamines can cause coronary vasospasm and ischemia

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have early heart disease, a heart attack before age 55 in a man or 65 in a woman, or sudden cardiac death?
key_questions.looking_for: Premature coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac death in a first-degree relative raises coronary risk

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or use tobacco?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or recent tobacco smoking is a strong coronary and venous thromboembolism risk factor

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy raises venous thromboembolism risk and must be known before imaging or medications that are contraindicated in pregnancy

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent trauma, heavy lifting, or a new strenuous exercise routine?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent trauma or heavy lifting suggests musculoskeletal or chest wall pain

reasoning_points: Characterizes the pain by onset, location, quality, radiation, duration, and provoking and relieving factors
Identifies red-flag features: pressure-like pain with diaphoresis, tearing pain maximal at onset radiating to the back, pleuritic pain with dyspnea and tachycardia, or syncope
Assesses coronary risk factors including prior coronary disease, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, tobacco use, and family history of premature coronary disease
Assesses venous thromboembolism risk factors including recent surgery, immobilization, long travel, active cancer, and prior venous thromboembolism
Considers the broad differential including acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, pericarditis, pneumothorax, pneumonia, reflux, costochondritis, and panic attack
Recognizes that reproducible chest wall tenderness does not fully exclude a cardiac cause
Orders an ECG within 10 minutes of arrival when acute coronary syndrome is suspected
Uses serial high-sensitivity troponin testing rather than a single value to detect acute myocardial injury
Confirms pregnancy status before imaging or medications that are contraindicated in pregnancy
Does not delay reperfusion for a patient with ST-segment elevation on ECG

easy: Classic substernal pressure with exertion, radiation to the left arm or jaw, and diaphoresis in a patient with coronary risk factors
Sudden pleuritic pain with dyspnea and tachycardia after recent surgery or long travel
Sharp positional pain that improves leaning forward with a pericardial friction rub after a viral illness
Burning postprandial pain relieved by antacids in a younger patient without coronary risk factors
medium: Older adult with dyspnea and weakness but no classic chest pain
Patient with diabetes and blunted anginal pain presenting with dyspnea alone
Reproducible chest wall tenderness in a patient who also has coronary risk factors
Pleuritic pain with clear lungs and no dyspnea where pulmonary embolism and musculoskeletal causes compete
Young woman with chest tightness, palpitations, and anxiety where panic attack and coronary causes compete
hard: Sudden tearing pain maximal at onset radiating to the back with a blood pressure differential between arms
Hypotension with distended neck veins and unilateral absent breath sounds
Chest pain with syncope or near-syncope suggesting arrhythmia, massive pulmonary embolism, or dissection
Pregnant patient with pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea where pulmonary embolism must be considered
Immunocompromised patient with blunted symptoms and possible pneumonia
Patient with renal impairment and chest pain where contrast imaging requires careful consideration
